PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Inflammation (ac:
Overview — The Response to Injury

Inflammation is the tissue response to injury or infection that delivers defence cells and mediators to the site. It is either acute (rapid, short-lived) or chronic (prolonged, with destruction and repair).

🔬 Image slot — acute vs chronic inflammation — neutrophil-rich oedematous tissue versus a mononuclear infiltrate with fibrosis
Acute
  • Minutes–days; neutrophil-dominant
  • Vascular + cellular events → exudate/oedema
Chronic
  • Weeks–years; macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells
  • Simultaneous tissue destruction + repair/fibrosis
The five cardinal signs: rubor (redness), calor (heat), tumor (swelling), dolor (pain) and functio laesa (loss of function).
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — inflamed tissue — acute shows neutrophils, oedema and vascular congestion; chronic shows lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages and fibrosis
  • Acute: abundant neutrophils, tissue oedema, dilated congested vessels, and fibrin.
  • Chronic: lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages, with fibrosis and granulation tissue.
  • Pus/abscess = a collection of neutrophils and necrotic debris.
Neutrophils = acute; mononuclear cells (macrophages/lymphocytes/plasma cells) + fibrosis = chronic. The dominant cell tells you the tempo.
Acute Inflammation — Vascular & Cellular Events
Vascular
  • Transient vasoconstriction → vasodilation (histamine, NO) → heat/redness
  • Increased permeability → protein-rich exudate & oedema; stasis
Cellular
  • Neutrophil recruitment then phagocytosis

The neutrophil recruitment cascade:

1
Margination & rollingE/P-selectins – sialyl-Lewis X on PSGL-1
2
Firm adhesionLFA-1/Mac-1 (CD18) – ICAM-1
3
Transmigration (diapedesis)PECAM-1
4
ChemotaxisC5a, LTB4, IL-8, bacterial peptides
Chemokines switch integrins to high-affinity, converting rolling into firm arrest. Permeability rises mainly by endothelial contraction (histamine/bradykinin, immediate-transient, venules) ± direct injury. Exudate (protein-rich, SG >1.020; clinically Light’s criteria) vs transudate (protein-poor, pressure-driven).
Patterns of acute inflammation: serous (effusion/blister), fibrinous (e.g. pericarditis), suppurative/purulent (abscess), ulcer, and membranous/pseudomembranous (e.g. C. difficile).
The Inflammatory Cells
Neutrophils
Acute first responders; 3–5-lobed nucleus; phagocytose then die → pus (>5 lobes = hypersegmented, B12/folate)
Macrophages
Chronic; phagocytose, present antigen, secrete cytokines/growth factors; become epithelioid/giant cells. M1 (IFN-γ/LPS) microbicidal vs M2 (IL-4/13) repair/fibrosis
Lymphocytes & plasma cells
Adaptive immunity; plasma cells secrete antibody (Russell bodies = packed Ig)
Eosinophils / mast cells
Eosinophils in parasites & allergy; mast cells release histamine
Neutrophil = acute; macrophage/lymphocyte/plasma cell = chronic; eosinophil = allergy/parasite. The infiltrate identifies the process.
Chronic Inflammation
  • Driven by persistent infection (e.g. TB), autoimmunity, foreign material, or prolonged toxin exposure.
  • Characterised by a mononuclear infiltrate with ongoing tissue destruction and attempted repair occurring together.
  • Granulation tissue (new capillaries + fibroblasts + inflammatory cells) forms, maturing into fibrosis/scar.
Chronic inflammation can follow unresolved acute inflammation or begin insidiously (e.g. TB, rheumatoid arthritis); prolonged inflammation (IL-6 → SAA) can deposit AA (reactive) amyloid. Granulomatous inflammation is a distinct pattern (covered separately). Defects: LAD-1 (CD18 integrin → no pus, delayed cord separation); CGD (NADPH oxidase → catalase-positive infections).
Mediators, Outcomes & Systemic Effects
Key mediators
Histamine/serotonin (vasodilation/permeability), prostaglandins (pain/fever), leukotrienes, PAF, NO & ROS, bradykinin, complement (C3a/C5a anaphylatoxins, C3b opsonin, MAC), cytokines (TNF, IL-1, IL-6)
Outcomes
Resolution, abscess (pus), healing with fibrosis, or progression to chronic inflammation
Systemic effects
Fever (IL-1/IL-6/TNF → PGE₂), acute-phase proteins (CRP, from IL-6), neutrophilia (bacterial) / lymphocytosis (viral)
Arachidonic acid cascade: membrane phospholipid →(PLA₂)→ arachidonic acid → COX → prostaglandins/thromboxane or LOX → leukotrienes. NSAIDs block COX (aspirin irreversibly, → pro-resolving lipoxins); steroids block PLA₂ (both arms). CRP is an IL-6-driven acute-phase marker.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Neutrophils = acute; macrophages + lymphocytes + plasma cells (+ fibrosis) = chronic.
Cardinal signs: rubor, calor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa.
Acute = vascular (vasodilation + permeability → exudate) + cellular (neutrophil recruitment).
Recruitment cascade: margination/rolling (selectins) → adhesion (integrins) → transmigration → chemotaxis.
Exudate = protein-rich (inflammation); transudate = protein-poor (pressure).
Chronic inflammation = destruction + repair together → granulation tissue & fibrosis.
Mediators: histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, C3a/C5a, TNF/IL-1/IL-6; pus = neutrophils + debris.
Systemic: fever (PGE₂), CRP (IL-6), neutrophilia (bacterial) vs lymphocytosis (viral).
Arachidonic acid: PLA₂ → COX (prostaglandins) / LOX (leukotrienes); steroids block PLA₂, NSAIDs block COX.
LAD-1 (CD18) = no pus; CGD (NADPH oxidase) = catalase-positive infections; chronic inflammation → AA amyloid.
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granuloma Format:
Overview — An Organised Macrophage Response

A granuloma is an organised nodular collection of epithelioid histiocytes (activated macrophages), often with multinucleate giant cells and a rim of lymphocytes. Immune granulomas (TB, sarcoid, fungi) are a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction; foreign-body granulomas form around inert material without T-cell sensitisation.

🔬 Image slot — granuloma — a nodule of epithelioid macrophages and a multinucleate giant cell, surrounded by a cuff of lymphocytes
  • It forms in response to persistent or poorly degradable antigen that ordinary inflammation cannot clear.
  • It is cell-mediated — driven by CD4 Th1 lymphocytes and macrophages.
The purpose is to wall off an agent the body cannot eliminate (e.g. TB bacilli, foreign material). Granulomatous ≠ infection: sarcoidosis, Crohn’s, GPA, foreign-body and drug reactions are all non-infective causes.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — granuloma histology — pale epithelioid macrophages with elongated pink cytoplasm, a Langhans giant cell, and a peripheral lymphocyte cuff; caseation if TB
  • A nodular aggregate of epithelioid macrophages — pale cells with abundant elongated pink cytoplasm (resembling epithelium).
  • Multinucleate giant cells and a surrounding rim of lymphocytes, sometimes with fibrosis.
  • Look for central caseous (cheese-like) necrosis — if present, think TB/fungal.
Epithelioid macrophages + giant cells + lymphocyte rim → granuloma. Then decide caseating vs non-caseating, which narrows the cause.
How a Granuloma Forms
1
Macrophage engulfs antigenpersistent/indigestible agent
2
IL-12 → CD4 Th1macrophage IL-12 drives Th1 → IFN-γ
3
Macrophage activationbecome epithelioid; fuse into giant cells
4
Walled-off granulomamaintained by TNF
Macrophage IL-12 → Th1 → IFN-γ activates macrophages; TNF maintains the granuloma. Anti-TNF drugs risk reactivating latent TB. The caseous centre is hypoxic, acidic and nutrient-poor — it contains (but does not kill) dormant bacilli and resists antibiotic penetration.
Epithelioid Macrophages & Giant Cells
  • Epithelioid macrophages — activated macrophages with elongated pink cytoplasm; strong secretion but poor phagocytosis.
Langhans giant cell
Nuclei arranged in a peripheral horseshoe/ring — classic (especially TB)
Foreign-body giant cell
Nuclei scattered randomly; around foreign material (often polarisable)
Touton giant cell
Ring of nuclei with foamy lipid cytoplasm; in fat-rich/xanthomatous lesions
Giant cells = fused macrophages. Nuclear pattern names them: peripheral horseshoe (Langhans), random (foreign body), lipid-laden ring (Touton). Also osteoclast-type (bone) and Warthin–Finkeldey cells (measles). Reed–Sternberg cells are NOT granuloma giant cells.
Caseating vs Non-Caseating & Causes
🔬 Image slot — caseating granuloma (central amorphous eosinophilic necrosis, TB) vs non-caseating granuloma (compact, no necrosis, sarcoidosis)
Caseating (necrotic centre)
  • TB (ZN stain for acid-fast bacilli), some fungi
  • Central amorphous eosinophilic “cheese-like” necrosis
Non-caseating (no necrosis)
  • Sarcoidosis, Crohn’s, foreign body, berylliosis
  • Leprosy (tuberculoid), rheumatoid nodule, PBC
  • Suppurative (neutrophil-rich centre): cat-scratch, LGV, Yersinia
Special stains find the cause: Ziehl–Neelsen (or the more sensitive fluorescent auramine–rhodamine) for acid-fast bacilli (TB), Grocott/PAS for fungi. Foreign material is often visible under polarised light.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Tuberculosis
Caseating granuloma + Langhans giant cells; ZN-positive AFB; Ghon focus/complex
Sarcoidosis
Non-caseating; bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy; BAL CD4:CD8 >3.5; raised ACE (non-specific); hypercalcaemia (macrophage 1α-hydroxylase → calcitriol). Löfgren & Heerfordt syndromes; asteroid/Schaumann bodies (not specific)
Crohn’s disease
Non-caseating granulomas in transmural bowel inflammation
Foreign-body reaction
Giant cells around suture/talc/keratin — often polarisable material
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Necrotising granulomas + vasculitis (c-ANCA/PR3)
Others
Leprosy, fungal infection, cat-scratch, syphilitic gumma, rheumatoid nodule, primary biliary cholangitis
Before starting anti-TNF therapy, screen for latent TB — TNF is needed to hold granulomas together, so blocking it can reactivate TB.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Granuloma = epithelioid macrophages + giant cells + lymphocyte rim — a type IV hypersensitivity reaction.
Formation needs CD4 Th1 → IFN-γ (activates macrophages) and TNF (maintains it).
Caseating (central necrosis) = TB/fungal; non-caseating = sarcoidosis, Crohn’s, foreign body, berylliosis.
Langhans giant cell = peripheral horseshoe nuclei (classic TB); foreign-body = random nuclei; Touton = lipid.
Epithelioid macrophage = activated, pink, secretory (poor phagocytosis).
TB: Ziehl–Neelsen stain for AFB; sarcoid: raised ACE, hypercalcaemia, asteroid/Schaumann bodies.
Fungi: Grocott/PAS stains; foreign material is polarisable.
Anti-TNF drugs risk TB reactivation — screen for latent TB first.
Immune granulomas = type IV (IL-12 → Th1 → IFN-γ); foreign-body granulomas are non-immune.
Sarcoid hypercalcaemia = macrophage 1α-hydroxylase → calcitriol; suppurative granuloma = cat-scratch/LGV.
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell Death (apop:
Overview — Two Ways Cells Die

Cells die in two main ways: apoptosis (regulated, “programmed”, tidy, no inflammation) and necrosis (uncontrolled, messy, with inflammation).

🔬 Image slot — apoptosis vs necrosis — a shrunken cell with condensed nucleus and apoptotic bodies versus a swollen cell with ruptured membrane and inflammation
Apoptosis
  • Single cells; shrink; membrane intact
  • Energy (ATP)-dependent; no inflammation
Necrosis
  • Groups of cells; swell; membrane ruptures
  • ATP-depleted; contents leak → inflammation
Apoptosis is a quiet, controlled suicide; necrosis is a violent, inflammatory accident. Apoptosis can be physiological or pathological; necrosis is always pathological.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — cell death histology — apoptotic bodies (shrunken, condensed nuclei, no inflammation) vs necrotic tissue with karyolysis and neutrophils
  • Apoptosis: shrunken, deeply eosinophilic cells with condensed/fragmented nuclei and apoptotic bodies — no inflammation.
  • Necrosis: swollen cells, fading/absent nuclei (karyolysis), and a surrounding inflammatory infiltrate.
  • The necrosis pattern (ghost outlines, liquefaction, caseation) points to the cause.
Shrunken single cells with no inflammation = apoptosis; swollen groups with inflammation = necrosis.
Apoptosis — Features & Pathways
  • Morphology: cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation (pyknosis), nuclear fragmentation (karyorrhexis), and membrane-bound apoptotic bodies phagocytosed by neighbours (so no inflammation).
  • DNA is cut at internucleosomal sites → a “ladder” pattern (vs a random smear in necrosis).
  • Dying cells flip phosphatidylserine to the outer leaflet as an “eat-me” signal (basis of annexin V detection). The intrinsic pathway can also kill caspase-independently via AIF/endonuclease G.
Intrinsic (mitochondrial)
  • Triggered by DNA damage / growth-factor withdrawal
  • BCL2 family balance: anti (BCL2/BCL-XL/MCL1) vs BAX/BAK + BH3-only (BID/BIM/PUMA)
  • BAX/BAK → MOMP → cytochrome c + APAF-1 + procaspase-9 = apoptosome → caspase 9
Extrinsic (death receptor)
  • Fas/FasL or TNF receptor → FADD → DISC → caspase 8
  • Caspase 8 cleaves BID → tBID, cross-linking to the intrinsic pathway
Both pathways converge on executioner caspases (3, 6, 7). p53 triggers apoptosis after DNA damage; BCL2 inhibits it (overexpressed in follicular lymphoma).
Necrosis & Its Patterns
🔬 Image slot — necrosis patterns — coagulative (ghost outlines), liquefactive, caseous, fat (saponification) and fibrinoid necrosis
Coagulative
Architecture preserved (ghost outlines); ischaemic infarcts of most organs (heart, kidney)
Liquefactive
Enzymatic digestion to liquid; brain infarct and abscess (pus)
Caseous
“Cheese-like” amorphous necrosis; TB and other granulomas
Fat necrosis
Pancreatitis (saponification) and trauma (e.g. breast)
Fibrinoid
Bright-pink fibrin & plasma proteins in vessel walls: immune-complex-driven in some vasculitides (PAN); plasma insudation in malignant hypertension/pre-eclampsia
Gangrene (clinical term)
Not a distinct mechanism: dry = coagulative (ischaemia); wet = + infection/liquefactive; gas = Clostridium
Nuclear changes progress: pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis. Coagulative = infarct; caseous = TB. Exception: the brain infarcts by liquefaction (high lipid, little stroma) despite being ischaemic.
Reversible → irreversible injury turns on mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP) opening, severe membrane damage and Ca2+ overload. Regulated necrosis: necroptosis (RIPK1/3→MLKL), pyroptosis (inflammasome→caspase-1→gasdermin-D + IL-1β), ferroptosis (iron/lipid peroxidation, GPX4 failure). Reperfusion injury is mainly ROS/free-radical-mediated.
Apoptosis vs Necrosis — The Contrast
FeatureApoptosisNecrosis
TriggerPhysiological or pathologicalAlways pathological
Cell sizeShrinksSwells
MembraneIntact (apoptotic bodies)Ruptured
InflammationNoneYes
EnergyATP-dependentATP-depleted
ExtentSingle cellsGroups of cells
DNALadder (internucleosomal)Random smear
One line: apoptosis = shrink, intact membrane, no inflammation, single cells, energy-dependent; necrosis = swell, rupture, inflammation, groups, energy-depleted.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Councilman bodies
Apoptotic hepatocytes (= acidophil bodies) in viral hepatitis and yellow fever — a classic apoptosis example
Myocardial infarction
Coagulative necrosis of ischaemic myocardium
Cerebral infarct
Liquefactive necrosis of brain tissue
Cancer — apoptosis evasion
BCL2 overexpression (follicular lymphoma, t(14;18)) or p53 loss lets cells escape apoptosis
Physiological apoptosis
Embryogenesis (digit separation), immune-cell selection, menstruation, hormone-dependent involution
Excess cell death
Neurodegeneration (apoptosis); ischaemia–reperfusion injury is mainly ROS/free-radical-mediated necrosis with Ca2+ overload (apoptosis contributes)
Too little apoptosis → cancer/autoimmunity; too much apoptosis → neurodegeneration. Its regulation is central to disease.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Apoptosis = programmed, single cells, shrinkage, pyknosis/karyorrhexis, apoptotic bodies, no inflammation, ATP-dependent, membrane intact.
Necrosis = uncontrolled, groups, swelling, membrane rupture, inflammation, ATP-depleted.
Intrinsic (mitochondrial; BCL2 / cytochrome c / caspase 9) vs extrinsic (Fas/TNF / caspase 8) → executioner caspases (3/6/7).
p53 triggers apoptosis after DNA damage; BCL2 inhibits it (follicular lymphoma).
Necrosis types: coagulative (infarct/ghosts), liquefactive (brain/abscess), caseous (TB), fat (pancreatitis), fibrinoid (vasculitis), gangrene.
Necrotic nuclear changes: pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis.
Councilman body = apoptotic hepatocyte (viral hepatitis).
Apoptosis DNA = ladder; necrosis DNA = random smear.
Extrinsic caspase 8 → tBID links to intrinsic; irreversibility = MPTP opening; apoptotic “eat-me” = phosphatidylserine flip (annexin V).
Regulated necrosis: necroptosis (MLKL), pyroptosis (gasdermin-D), ferroptosis (GPX4); brain infarct = liquefactive (exception).
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neoplasia (benig:
Overview — Abnormal, Autonomous Growth

A neoplasm is an abnormal, autonomous, uncoordinated tissue growth that persists after the initiating stimulus is removed. Neoplasms are benign or malignant.

🔬 Image slot — benign vs malignant tumour — a well-circumscribed encapsulated mass versus an irregular infiltrative one with pleomorphic cells
Naming benign
  • Suffix -oma: adenoma, lipoma, leiomyoma, chondroma
Naming malignant
  • Epithelial → carcinoma (glandular = adeno-, squamous = SCC); mesenchymal → sarcoma
  • Leukaemia (blood/marrow) vs lymphoma (solid lymphoid); -blastoma = childhood embryonal (Wilms, neuro-, retino-)
Naming exceptions: melanoma, lymphoma, mesothelioma, seminoma, glioma/astrocytoma and hepatoma are malignant despite “-oma”. Teratoma = germ-cell tumour (mature = benign; immature = malignant). Hamartoma (disorganised native tissue) and choristoma (normal tissue at an ectopic site) are non-neoplastic.
How to Recognise Malignancy on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — malignant histology — pleomorphic hyperchromatic cells, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, prominent nucleoli, abnormal mitoses and invasion

Malignancy = anaplasia (loss of differentiation) plus invasion:

  • Pleomorphism — variation in cell/nuclear size and shape.
  • Hyperchromatic nuclei with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and prominent nucleoli.
  • Abnormal/frequent mitoses and tumour necrosis.
  • Infiltrative, irregular margins breaching the basement membrane.
Anaplasia + invasion through the basement membrane → malignant. A well-differentiated, encapsulated, non-invasive mass is benign.
Benign vs Malignant — The Contrast
FeatureBenignMalignant
DifferentiationWell-differentiated (resembles tissue)Variable / anaplastic
Growth rateSlow, few mitosesRapid, many/abnormal mitoses
BorderCircumscribed / encapsulatedInfiltrative, irregular
InvasionNoYes (breaches basement membrane)
MetastasisNeverYes (definitive)
NecrosisRareCommon
Metastasis is the definitive proof of malignancy; invasion separates invasive cancer from carcinoma in situ. Circumscription/encapsulation favours benignity but is not defining — some benign tumours are unencapsulated and some cancers look circumscribed. Invasion (with a desmoplastic stromal reaction) is the true discriminator.
Invasion, Metastasis & Routes of Spread
🔬 Image slot — progression — carcinoma in situ (basement membrane intact) advancing to invasive carcinoma breaching the basement membrane
  • Carcinoma in situ (full-thickness dysplasia, basement membrane intact) → invasive carcinoma (basement membrane breached). Dysplasia is reversible/pre-invasive; invasion is not.
  • Metastatic cascade: detachment (E-cadherin loss / EMT) → ECM invasion (MMPs) → intravasation → survival as emboli → extravasation → colonisation. Site is set by “seed & soil” (microenvironment) and mechanical/anatomical drainage.
Lymphatic
Typical of carcinomas → regional lymph nodes
Haematogenous
Typical of sarcomas (also carcinomas) → liver, lung, bone, brain
Transcoelomic
Across body cavities (e.g. ovarian cancer seeding the peritoneum)
Carcinoma → lymphatic; sarcoma → haematogenous (a generalisation). Exceptions: renal cell, follicular thyroid, hepatocellular and choriocarcinoma spread haematogenously.
Carcinogenesis, Grade & Stage
  • Cancer arises by stepwise accumulation of mutations: activation of oncogenes (gain of function — RAS, MYC, HER2), loss of tumour-suppressor genes (p53, RB, APC; Knudson two-hit — both alleles), and defects in caretaker/DNA-repair genes (mismatch repair/Lynch, BRCA1/2). The adenoma–carcinoma sequence (APC→KRAS→p53) is the classic colorectal model.
  • Hallmarks of cancer (Hanahan–Weinberg): self-sufficient growth, insensitivity to anti-growth signals, evasion of apoptosis, limitless replication (telomerase), angiogenesis, invasion/metastasis — plus the 2011 additions: genome instability, tumour-promoting inflammation, deregulated energetics (Warburg), avoiding immune destruction.
Grade
  • How abnormal the cells look (differentiation): low vs high grade
Stage (TNM)
  • How far it has spread: Tumour size, Nodes, Metastasis
  • Usually the stronger prognostic factor
Grade = differentiation (G1–G3; Nottingham/Bloom–Richardson for breast, Gleason for prostate); Stage = spread (TNM, incl. Tis in situ; sentinel node biopsy). Stage usually predicts prognosis better.
Carcinogens: chemical (PAHs, aromatic amines→bladder, aflatoxin→liver), radiation (UV, ionising), and oncogenic microbes: HPV (cervix/oropharynx), EBV (Burkitt, nasopharyngeal), HBV/HCV (HCC), HTLV-1, HHV-8, H. pylori (gastric/MALT).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Immunohistochemistry
Cytokeratin = epithelial (carcinoma); vimentin = mesenchymal; S100 = melanoma/nerve; CD45 = lymphoid
Serum tumour markers
PSA (prostate), AFP (HCC/yolk-sac), CEA (colorectal), CA-125 (ovarian), β-hCG (choriocarcinoma/germ-cell) — mainly for monitoring, not screening
Paraneoplastic syndromes
Hormone/cytokine secretion (e.g. SIADH, hypercalcaemia, Cushing’s) remote from the tumour
Cancer cachexia
Weight loss & wasting (TNF/cytokine-mediated)
Local effects
Compression, obstruction, ulceration/bleeding — even benign tumours can be dangerous by location (e.g. meningioma)
BCL2 / p53 in cancer
Evasion of apoptosis via BCL2 overexpression or p53 loss
Field change / progression
Dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinoma over time
⭐ Exam Pearls
Malignant hallmarks: anaplasia (pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, high N:C ratio, prominent nucleoli, abnormal mitoses), invasion, metastasis, rapid growth, necrosis.
Metastasis = definitive proof of malignancy; basement-membrane invasion = key distinguishing feature.
Benign = well-differentiated, encapsulated, non-invasive, slow.
Naming: -oma benign; carcinoma (epithelial), sarcoma (mesenchymal); exceptions melanoma/lymphoma/mesothelioma/seminoma.
Oncogenes (RAS/MYC/HER2) = gain of function; tumour suppressors (p53/RB/APC) = loss.
Grade = differentiation; Stage (TNM) = spread — stage usually matters most.
Carcinoma → lymphatic; sarcoma → haematogenous; transcoelomic (ovarian).
Carcinoma in situ (BM intact) vs invasive carcinoma (BM breached).
Hallmarks now include genome instability, tumour-promoting inflammation, Warburg energetics, immune evasion; Knudson two-hit for tumour suppressors.
Oncogenic microbes: HPV, EBV, HBV/HCV, HTLV-1, HHV-8, H. pylori; markers PSA/AFP/CEA/CA-125/hCG.
Metastatic cascade: E-cadherin loss/EMT → MMPs → intravasation → extravasation; site = seed & soil.
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metaplasia & Dys:
Overview — Adaptation & the Road to Cancer

Cells adapt to stress by changing size, number or type. Metaplasia and dysplasia are two such changes — metaplasia is a reversible change of cell type, while dysplasia is disordered, atypical growth on the road to cancer.

🔬 Image slot — adaptation spectrum — hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, metaplasia, then dysplasia progressing toward neoplasia
Hypertrophy / Hyperplasia
Bigger cells / more cells (permanent tissues — heart, skeletal muscle, neurons — can only hypertrophy)
Atrophy
Smaller / fewer cells
Metaplasia
One differentiated tissue type replaced by another via altered stem-cell differentiation (adaptive, potentially reversible)
Dysplasia
Disordered atypical growth — pre-malignant
Metaplasia is an adaptation; dysplasia is a step toward malignancy. Persistent metaplastic stress can progress to dysplasia, then cancer.
How to Recognise Them on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — metaplasia (one normal mature epithelium replaced by another) vs dysplasia (atypical, disordered cells with an intact basement membrane)
  • Metaplasia: one normal, mature epithelium replaced by another normal mature type (via reprogrammed stem cells, not transdifferentiation of mature cells) — e.g. goblet/columnar cells in the oesophagus.
  • Dysplasia: atypical cells with loss of maturation/polarity and mitoses above the basal layer — but the basement membrane is intact.
Metaplasia = a different but orderly, mature epithelium; dysplasia = disorganised, atypical cells (still confined by the basement membrane).
Metaplasia

Metaplasia is the (potentially reversible) replacement of one differentiated cell type by another better suited to the stress, by reprogramming of stem/reserve cells (mature cells do not transdifferentiate). Intestinal metaplasia is driven by CDX2; vitamin A deficiency causes squamous metaplasia.

Barrett’s oesophagus
Squamous → metaplastic columnar epithelium, from acid reflux (UK/BSG needs only columnar-lined oesophagus; US/CAP requires goblet cells/intestinal metaplasia)
Bronchial (smoking)
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar → squamous (loses cilia)
Cervical transformation zone
Columnar → squamous metaplasia (physiological)
Gastric
Intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells) from chronic H. pylori
Bladder
Transitional → squamous (schistosomiasis/stones) or glandular metaplasia
Apocrine (breast)
A benign, NOT premalignant metaplasia — metaplasia is not always a cancer road
Mesenchymal metaplasia
Connective tissue → bone/cartilage (myositis ossificans — reactive); myeloid metaplasia = extramedullary haematopoiesis (myelofibrosis)
Metaplasia often sacrifices protection (e.g. loss of cilia in the bronchi) and, if the stress persists, becomes the substrate for dysplasia. It is only potentially reversible — Barrett’s and gastric intestinal metaplasia rarely fully regress.
Dysplasia
🔬 Image slot — dysplastic epithelium — nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, increased mitoses and loss of polarity, with an intact basement membrane
  • Dysplasia = disordered epithelial growth with cytological atypia and architectural disarray, but NO invasion (basement membrane intact). It is pre-malignant.
  • Features: pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, increased N:C ratio, increased/abnormal mitoses, loss of polarity and maturation.
  • Graded low- vs high-grade; high-grade dysplasia overlaps with carcinoma in situ (full-thickness change, BM intact) — though “CIS” is avoided in glandular/GI sites. Grading is subjective/poorly reproducible; p53 and DNA aneuploidy aid objectivity.
Low-grade dysplasia may reverse if the stimulus is removed, but higher grades carry a rising risk of progression to invasive carcinoma.
The Progression Sequence
1
Normalhealthy epithelium
2
Metaplasiaadaptive cell-type change
3
Dysplasiaatypia, BM intact
4
Carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinomaBM breached at invasion
Metaplasia and dysplasia are (potentially) reversible; invasion is not. The whole point of surveillance is to catch dysplasia before it becomes invasive cancer.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Barrett’s oesophagus
Intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma; monitored by surveillance endoscopy
Cervix (CIN)
The actively metaplastic transformation zone is the substrate where HPV drives dysplasia (CIN 1–3); detected by the smear
Bronchus
Squamous metaplasia → dysplasia → squamous cell carcinoma (smoking)
Stomach
Intestinal metaplasia (H. pylori) → dysplasia → gastric adenocarcinoma
Actinic keratosis
Sun-induced epidermal dysplasia → cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
Leukoplakia / erythroplakia
Leukoplakia = white oral patch, a clinical diagnosis of exclusion (biopsy; variable dysplasia); erythroplakia (red patch) carries a much higher dysplasia/SCC risk
Recognising metaplasia/dysplasia enables screening & surveillance (e.g. cervical smears, Barrett’s endoscopy) to intervene before invasive cancer develops.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Metaplasia = reversible change of one mature cell type to another (adaptive, stem-cell reprogramming).
Classics: Barrett’s (squamous→columnar/goblet), bronchial (columnar→squamous), cervical transformation zone, gastric intestinal metaplasia.
Dysplasia = disordered growth + cytological atypia, basement membrane intact, pre-malignant.
Dysplasia is graded low/high; high-grade dysplasia = carcinoma in situ.
Sequence: normal → metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinoma.
Metaplasia & dysplasia are (potentially) reversible; invasion is not.
Dysplasia is not invasion (BM intact); invasion through the BM defines malignancy.
Myositis ossificans = mesenchymal metaplasia (CT → bone); actinic keratosis = premalignant dysplasia.
Metaplasia = stem-cell reprogramming (not mature transdifferentiation); intestinal metaplasia driven by CDX2; vitamin A deficiency → squamous metaplasia.
Apocrine metaplasia (breast) is benign — metaplasia isn’t always premalignant; leukoplakia is a clinical term (biopsy), erythroplakia is higher-risk.
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibrosis & Repai:
Overview — Regeneration vs Repair

After injury, tissue heals in one of two ways: regeneration (restoring normal tissue) or repair by fibrosis (replacing it with a collagen scar).

🔬 Image slot — healing routes — regeneration restoring normal architecture vs repair laying down a fibrous scar
Regeneration
  • Needs labile/stable cells + an intact framework
  • Restores normal structure & function
Repair (fibrosis)
  • When cells are permanent or the framework is destroyed
  • Leaves a collagen scar
Regenerate if you can, scar if you must. Whether tissue regenerates depends on the cell type and whether the connective-tissue framework survived.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — healing tissue — early granulation tissue (capillaries + fibroblasts + inflammatory cells) versus mature scar (dense collagen, few cells/vessels)
  • Granulation tissue (early): new capillaries, plump fibroblasts, loose matrix and inflammatory cells — pink and granular.
  • Mature scar (late): dense collagen with few cells/vessels and no adnexa (no hair follicles, sweat/sebaceous glands) or elastic tissue.
  • Fibrosis: excess collagen (blue on Masson’s trichrome) distorting normal architecture.
Capillaries + fibroblasts + inflammatory cells = granulation tissue; dense acellular collagen = scar. Trichrome stains collagen. NB granulation tissue ≠ granuloma (an epithelioid-macrophage nodule).
Cell Regenerative Capacity
Labile
Continuously dividing — epidermis, gut epithelium, bone marrow; regenerate well
Stable
Quiescent but can divide — liver, kidney tubules, fibroblasts; regenerate if framework intact
Permanent
Cannot divide — neurons & cardiac muscle (heal by scar). Skeletal muscle has limited repair via satellite (Pax7) cells; large defects still scar
Labile & stable cells can regenerate; permanent cells scar. This is why a healed myocardial infarct is fibrous scar, not new muscle.
Granulation Tissue, Collagen & Wound Healing
1
Haemostasisclot/fibrin
2
Inflammationneutrophils → macrophages
3
Proliferationgranulation, angiogenesis, re-epithelialisation
4
Remodellingcollagen III → I; scar matures
  • Myofibroblasts (α-SMA-positive) contract the wound. Early type III collagen is replaced by stronger type I by MMPs (zinc-dependent), balanced by TIMPs. Wound strength: ~10% at 1 week, rising to a plateau of ~70–80% by 3 months — never 100%.
  • The fibrin/fibronectin clot forms the provisional matrix scaffold for cell migration; hypoxia → HIF-1α → VEGF drives angiogenesis by endothelial sprouting. Type IV collagen = basement membrane.
Primary intention
  • Clean, apposed edges (surgical); little tissue loss; epithelium bridges in ~24–48 h
  • Fast, minimal granulation, small scar
Secondary intention
  • Large/gaping wound; abundant granulation
  • Wound contraction (myofibroblasts), larger scar, slower
Growth Factors & Fibrosis
VEGF
Drives angiogenesis (new vessels)
PDGF
Recruits fibroblasts & smooth muscle
TGF-β
The key driver of fibrosis — stimulates fibroblasts & collagen deposition
FGF / EGF
Angiogenesis, fibroblast & epithelial proliferation

Fibrosis is excessive collagen deposition replacing normal tissue and impairing function, driven by chronic injury/inflammation and TGF-β-activated (myo)fibroblasts:

  • Liver cirrhosis (quiescent stellate/Ito cells store vitamin A; on activation they lose it & secrete collagen), pulmonary fibrosis, post-MI cardiac fibrosis, chronic kidney disease.
TGF-β is the master fibrogenic cytokine. Persistent activation converts a helpful repair response into pathological, function-destroying fibrosis.
Abnormal Healing & Clinical Correlate
Hypertrophic scar
Excess collagen within the original wound margins
Keloid
Disorganised collagen (↑ type I:III) extending beyond the wound; genetic/ethnic predisposition (pigmented skin; sternum/earlobe/deltoid); recurs — intralesional steroid/silicone/excision + RT
Contracture
Excessive myofibroblast contraction (e.g. across a joint after burns)
Dehiscence / chronic ulcer
Wound rupture or failure to heal
Impaired-healing factors
Diabetes, steroids, infection, ischaemia, poor nutrition
Scurvy (vitamin C)
Defective collagen cross-linking → poor wound strength & bleeding
Vitamin C is a cofactor for collagen hydroxylation/cross-linking, so its deficiency (scurvy) causes weak scars, bleeding gums and poor healing.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Regeneration needs labile/stable cells + intact framework; otherwise repair by fibrosis (scar).
Cell types: labile (epidermis/gut/marrow), stable (liver/kidney), permanent (neurons/cardiac/skeletal muscle → scar).
Granulation tissue = angiogenesis + fibroblasts + inflammatory cells; myofibroblasts contract the wound.
Collagen type III (early) → type I (mature scar); strength reaches ~80%.
Primary intention (apposed, small scar) vs secondary intention (gaping, granulation + contraction).
TGF-β = key fibrosis driver; VEGF (angiogenesis), PDGF (fibroblasts).
Keloid = collagen beyond wound margins; hypertrophic scar = within.
Poor healing: diabetes, steroids, infection, ischaemia, vitamin C deficiency (scurvy).
Vitamin C = proline/lysine hydroxylation (+ Fe²⁺); cross-linking = lysyl oxidase (copper) — not vitamin C.
Permanent = neurons & cardiac; skeletal muscle repairs via satellite cells; liver regenerates by hepatocyte hyperplasia.
Strength: ~10% at 1 wk → ~80% by 3 mo, never 100%; remodelling by MMPs/TIMPs; myofibroblast = α-SMA.
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascular Patholo:
Overview — Disease of the Vessels

Vascular pathology underlies the biggest killers — myocardial infarction and stroke. Two processes dominate: atherosclerosis (chronic arterial intimal disease) and thrombosis (intravascular clot), which together cause ischaemia and infarction.

🔬 Image slot — vascular disease overview — an atherosclerotic plaque narrowing an artery, a superimposed thrombus, and downstream infarction
Atherosclerosis
  • Intimal plaques in large/medium arteries (one type of arteriosclerosis)
  • Causes stenosis & is the substrate for thrombosis
Thrombosis
  • Clot forming within a vessel
  • Can occlude locally or embolise
The lethal combination is a plaque that ruptures and triggers thrombosis, acutely occluding an artery (heart → MI; brain → stroke).
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — atheroma & thrombus — an intimal plaque with a fibrous cap over a lipid/necrotic core with cholesterol clefts, and a thrombus showing lines of Zahn
  • Atheroma: an intimal plaque with a fibrous cap over a lipid/necrotic core containing foam cells and cholesterol clefts.
  • Thrombus: attached to the vessel wall, showing lines of Zahn (alternating pale platelet/fibrin and red-cell layers).
  • A post-mortem clot is not attached, is gelatinous ('chicken-fat/currant-jelly'), and lacks lines of Zahn.
Fibrous cap + lipid core with cholesterol clefts = atheroma; wall-attached clot with lines of Zahn = (antemortem) thrombus.
Atherosclerosis — Pathogenesis & Plaque
1
Endothelial injuryHTN, smoking, lipids, diabetes
2
LDL entry & oxidationmacrophages engulf → foam cells
3
Fatty streakearliest lesion (reversible)
4
Fibrous plaquesmooth muscle + cap over necrotic lipid core
  • Plaque = a fibrous cap (smooth muscle cells that migrated from the media + collagen) over a necrotic lipid core (cholesterol clefts, foam cells, debris) ± calcification. Macrophages take up oxLDL via scavenger receptors (unregulated); T cells and PDGF drive the chronic inflammation and SMC migration.
  • Favoured sites: abdominal aorta, coronary, popliteal, carotid, circle of Willis.
Stable plaque (thick cap, small core) → stable angina; vulnerable plaque (thin cap, large lipid core) → rupture → thrombosis → acute coronary syndrome.
Arteriosclerosis is the umbrella: atherosclerosis (intima); Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis (media calcifies, lumen NOT narrowed, benign); arteriolosclerosis — hyaline (benign HTN/diabetes) & hyperplastic “onion-skin” (malignant HTN).
Thrombosis — Virchow’s Triad
Endothelial injury
e.g. ruptured plaque, vasculitis, trauma
Abnormal flow
Stasis (immobility, AF) or turbulence
Hypercoagulability
Inherited (Factor V Leiden) or acquired (surgery, cancer, pregnancy)
Arterial thrombus
  • High flow; forms on a ruptured plaque
  • Pale (platelet/fibrin-rich); prominent lines of Zahn → MI/stroke
Venous thrombus
  • Stasis-driven; red (RBC-rich)
  • DVT; can propagate & embolise (→ PE)
Lines of Zahn (alternating platelet/fibrin and red-cell layers) indicate an antemortem thrombus vs a post-mortem clot. They need flow, so are prominent in arterial/cardiac thrombi and often inapparent in venous (stasis) thrombi. Fate: propagation, embolism, dissolution, or organisation/recanalisation.
Embolism & Infarction
🔬 Image slot — embolism & infarction — a thromboembolus lodging in a vessel and downstream infarction (white/anaemic vs red/haemorrhagic)
  • Embolism = a detached intravascular mass carried to a distant site. Most are thromboemboli: venous → pulmonary embolism (a large saddle embolus at the bifurcation can cause sudden death); arterial → systemic (brain, limbs). Others: fat (fractures; respiratory/neuro/petechiae at 24–72 h), amniotic fluid (→ DIC), air (~100 mL venous), septic, tumour, cholesterol.
  • Infarction = ischaemic necrosis from occlusion (usually coagulative; the brain is liquefactive); infarcts are classically wedge-shaped (occluded vessel at the apex, organ surface at the base). Reperfusion can worsen injury (free radicals) and convert a white infarct to haemorrhagic.
White (anaemic) infarct
  • Solid, end-artery organs: heart, kidney, spleen
Red (haemorrhagic) infarct
  • Loose tissue / dual supply: lung, bowel; venous occlusion
White infarct = solid end-artery organ (heart/kidney/spleen); red infarct = lung/bowel or venous occlusion.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Myocardial infarction / stroke
Plaque rupture → coronary/cerebral artery thrombosis
Peripheral arterial disease
Atherosclerotic stenosis → claudication, critical limb ischaemia
Aneurysm (distinct types)
AAA (infrarenal; MMP-mediated medial destruction; smoking = strongest RF); dissection (cystic medial degeneration/Marfan, not atherosclerosis); syphilitic (ascending, vasa vasorum endarteritis); berry (circle of Willis/ADPKD); mycotic (infective)
DVT & pulmonary embolism
Venous stasis (immobility, surgery, cancer, pregnancy/OCP) → leg DVT → PE; Wells score, D-dimer (sensitive), Doppler US
Risk factors
Modifiable: smoking, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia; non-modifiable: age, male sex, family history
Treatment logic
Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel) for arterial; anticoagulants (heparin/LMWH, DOACs, warfarin) for venous; thrombolysis (alteplase) for acute occlusion; statins & risk-factor control
Arterial disease is platelet-driven (antiplatelets); venous thrombosis is coagulation-driven (anticoagulants). Statins stabilise plaques and lower LDL.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Atheroma = intimal plaque (fibrous cap + lipid/necrotic core, foam cells, cholesterol clefts) in large/medium arteries; response-to-injury.
Foam cells = lipid-laden macrophages; the fatty streak is the earliest lesion.
Vulnerable plaque = thin cap + large lipid core → rupture → thrombosis → ACS.
Virchow’s triad: endothelial injury, abnormal flow (stasis/turbulence), hypercoagulability.
Arterial thrombus = pale, platelet-rich, on plaque, lines of Zahn; venous = red, stasis-driven (DVT).
Lines of Zahn = antemortem thrombus (vs unattached post-mortem clot).
Embolism: thromboembolism (DVT → PE), plus fat, air, amniotic; white infarct (heart/kidney/spleen) vs red (lung/bowel).
Antiplatelets for arterial; anticoagulants for venous disease.
Arteriosclerosis = atherosclerosis (intima) + Mönckeberg (media) + arteriolosclerosis (hyaline/hyperplastic HTN).
Aneurysms differ: AAA (MMP/infrarenal), dissection (cystic medial degeneration/Marfan), syphilitic (ascending), berry (circle of Willis/ADPKD).
Fat embolism triad at 24–72 h; amniotic fluid → DIC; saddle embolus = sudden death; infarcts are wedge-shaped.
PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Common Tumour Hi:
Overview — Three Carcinoma Patterns

Most carcinomas fall into three recognisable morphologies. Spotting the pattern of differentiation points you to the tissue of origin:

🔬 Image slot — three carcinoma patterns — gland-forming adenocarcinoma, keratin-pearl squamous cell carcinoma, and papillary urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma
Adenocarcinoma
Glandular differentiation — forms glands & makes mucin
Squamous cell carcinoma
Squamous differentiation — keratin pearls & intercellular bridges
Transitional cell (urothelial)
Urothelial differentiation — papillary/thickened transitional epithelium
Glands + mucin = adeno; keratin pearls + intercellular bridges = SCC; papillary urothelium = transitional cell carcinoma.
How to Recognise Them on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — discriminators — mucin-filled glands, keratin whorls with intercellular bridges, and papillary fronds of thickened urothelium
  • Adenocarcinoma: gland/tubule/acinar formation, mucin vacuoles, sometimes signet-ring cells.
  • SCC: nests of eosinophilic cells with keratin pearls (concentric keratin whorls) and intercellular bridges.
  • Transitional cell carcinoma: papillary fronds or thickened urothelium (>7 layers) with loss of polarity and atypia.
Grade each by differentiation (well → poorly differentiated) — how closely it still resembles the parent tissue.
Adenocarcinoma
  • A malignant epithelial tumour of glandular epithelium that forms glands and/or produces mucin.
  • Clues: gland/cribriform architecture, mucin vacuoles, and signet-ring cells (diffuse gastric type).
  • Common sites: GI (colon, stomach, pancreas, lower oesophagus), lung (peripheral), breast, prostate, endometrium.
  • Markers: mucin (PAS/mucicarmine), CEA, and organ-specific stains — TTF-1 (lung), CDX2 (GI), PSA (prostate), ER (breast).
Barrett’s oesophagus → adenocarcinoma; peripheral lung tumour with TTF-1 → adenocarcinoma. Signet-ring cells signal diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma
🔬 Image slot — squamous cell carcinoma — nests of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls and visible intercellular bridges
  • A malignant epithelial tumour with squamous differentiation, arising from squamous epithelium or squamous metaplasia.
  • Hallmarks: keratin pearls, intercellular bridges (desmosomes), and individual-cell keratinisation.
  • Common sites: skin (UV), lung (central, smoking), head & neck/oral (smoking/alcohol/HPV), oesophagus (upper/mid), cervix (HPV), anus.
  • Markers: p40, p63, CK5/6.
Central lung SCC (smoking) can secrete PTHrP → hypercalcaemia. Keratin pearls + intercellular bridges name the tumour regardless of site.
Transitional Cell (Urothelial) Carcinoma
  • A malignant tumour of the urothelium (transitional epithelium); most arise in the bladder (also ureter, renal pelvis, urethra).
  • Histology: papillary fronds on fibrovascular cores, or flat lesions; thickened urothelium with loss of polarity, umbrella-cell loss and atypia.
  • Risk factors: smoking, aromatic amines (dye/rubber industry), cyclophosphamide.
  • Classic presentation: painless haematuria. Markers: GATA3, CK7, uroplakin.
Schistosomiasis of the bladder causes squamous cell carcinoma, not transitional cell carcinoma — a favourite exam twist.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Lung
Peripheral adenocarcinoma (TTF-1, non-smokers/women) vs central SCC (smoking, cavitating, PTHrP)
Oesophagus
Lower-third adenocarcinoma (Barrett’s) vs upper/mid SCC (smoking/alcohol)
Colon / pancreas
Adenocarcinoma (glandular, CEA/CA19-9)
Cervix / head & neck
Squamous cell carcinoma (HPV-related)
Bladder
Transitional cell carcinoma — painless haematuria; SCC if schistosomiasis
Prostate
Adenocarcinoma (PSA, Gleason grade, loss of basal cells)
Immunohistochemistry pins the primary when the morphology is ambiguous: TTF-1, CDX2, PSA, ER (adeno); p40/p63 (SCC); GATA3 (urothelial & breast).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Adenocarcinoma = glands + mucin (signet-ring in diffuse gastric); markers CEA, TTF-1 (lung), CDX2 (GI), PSA (prostate), ER (breast).
SCC = keratin pearls + intercellular bridges; p40/p63/CK5-6; skin, central lung, head & neck, upper oesophagus, cervix.
Transitional cell (urothelial) carcinoma = bladder, painless haematuria, papillary; smoking/aromatic amines; GATA3.
Lung: central SCC (smoking, PTHrP → hypercalcaemia) vs peripheral adeno (TTF-1).
Oesophagus: lower adeno (Barrett’s) vs upper/mid SCC.
Schistosomiasis → squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder (not TCC).
Grade = differentiation (well → poorly differentiated).
Pattern → origin: glands=adeno, keratin=SCC, papillary urothelium=TCC.
